title: Multiple Linear Regression II
description: Twenty recall cards on categorical predictors, joint inference, ANOVA, and interactions.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind binary variables?
cards.back: A factor with c categories is represented with c-1 binary indicators when an intercept is present; the omitted level is the reference.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind reference levels?
cards.back: Changing the omitted category changes coefficient interpretations and individual t-ratios, but not fitted values or the overall model fit.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind general linear hypothesis?
cards.back: Joint restrictions are expressed as H0: Cβ=d, with C chosen for the scientific question.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind partial f test?
cards.back: Compare a reduced nested model with a full model: F=((Error SS)reduced-(Error SS)full)/(p s²full).

cards.front: What is the key idea behind term life example?
cards.back: Testing MAR0 and MAR2 jointly gives F=3.235 with p=2 and 269 denominator degrees of freedom; the reported p-value is 0.0409.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind one-factor anova?
cards.back: The model yᵢⱼ=μⱼ+εᵢⱼ estimates each group mean by its sample average and partitions total variation into factor and error sums of squares.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind auto claims anova?
cards.back: For 18 risk classes and 6,773 claims, log-claim ANOVA reports Factor SS 39.2, Error SS 7729.0, and Error MS 1.14.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind ancova?
cards.back: A factor and covariate can have variable intercepts with a common slope, or both intercepts and slopes can vary by group.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind hospital costs?
cards.back: The pooled plot suggests a negative association, but DRG-specific relationships show why an omitted factor can mislead; the variable-slope test is F=13.535.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind interactions?
cards.back: Interactions permit effects such as slopes to differ by category; with two factors they can be interpreted as a combined factor.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind general linear model?
cards.back: Continuous, transformed, and categorical predictors can enter linearly in coefficients; coefficient estimates can be nonunique under linear dependence.

cards.front: What is the key idea behind unique fitted values?
cards.back: Even when parameter estimates are not unique, least-squares fitted values, residuals, and error sums of squares are unique.

cards.front: Why are only c-1 indicators used for a c-level factor with an intercept?
cards.back: All c indicators sum to one, creating perfect linear dependence with the intercept.

cards.front: What does a partial F test compare?
cards.back: A reduced model that imposes the null restrictions with a full nested model.

cards.front: What is the least-squares estimate of μⱼ in one-factor ANOVA?
cards.back: The group sample mean, ȳⱼ.

cards.front: What does an interaction allow in an ANCOVA model?
cards.back: The covariate effect, such as a slope, may differ across factor levels.

cards.front: What remains unique in a linearly dependent general linear model?
cards.back: Fitted values, residuals, and error sums of squares remain unique even if coefficients do not.

cards.front: ______ is the omitted factor category used as the baseline for interpreting indicator coefficients.
cards.back: The reference level.

cards.front: The factor sum of squares equals total SS minus ______.
cards.back: error SS.

cards.front: In the term-life example, marital status is assessed by testing ______ jointly.
cards.back: the MAR0 and MAR2 coefficients.
